items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6912: Improving Wearable PPG Monitoring with Morphology-Aware and Learning-Driven Heartbeat Detection
items.summary: Photoplethysmography (PPG) is a widely used, non-invasive technique for heart rate monitoring, but its reliability is often compromised by noise and motion artifacts (MAs). This study presents the Peakwise Correlation Pulse Detector (PCPD), an algorithm for detecting heartbeats directly from PPG signals without requiring electrocardiogram (ECG) signals during operation, evaluated here under clean and controlled synthetic pulse-free-noise conditions. PCPD follows a five-step pipeline: (1) signal segmentation with overlap, (2) sliding cross-correlation using high-quality heartbeat templates, (3) computation of the Minimum Correlation Curve (MCC), (4) feature extraction with machine learning-based classification, and (5) peak translation with constraint analysis. The method was evaluated on a clean dataset, comprising a newly collected PPG dataset with manually annotated signal quality and the publicly available BIDMC dataset, and on a noisy dataset that augments the clean data with synthetic pulse-free segments generated from band-limited Gaussian noise. This evaluation framework tests heartbeat detectors under ideal conditions and under a controlled non-informative-noise protocol. On clean signals, PCPD achieved balanced precision-recall scores of 99.13% on the proposed dataset (internal performance) and 97.04% on the independent BIDMC dataset. Under added synthetic pulse-free noise, PCPD achieved accuracies of 99.30% and 97.16% on the proposed and BIDMC datasets, respectively. In comparative experiments against eleven benchmark heartbeat detection algorithms, PCPD achieved the best performance among the evaluated implementations under the tested synthetic-noise protocol. These results support PCPD as a promising PPG-only peak detector and motivate further validation under real motion artifacts and for downstream signal quality assessment.

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6897: Multi-Wavelength PPG Amplitude Ratio Features for Cuffless Blood Pressure Estimation: An Exploratory Study
items.summary: Background: Cuffless blood pressure (BP) estimation from photoplethysmography (PPG) remains challenging. This exploratory study investigated whether curvature-derived waveform features from multiple PPG wavelengths, particularly amplitude ratios, are associated with cuff-based BP readings. Methods: Red, infrared, and green PPG signals were recorded for 90 s from 48 physician-screened volunteers (23 males and 25 females; mean age, 63.41 +/- 14.20 years). A single automated upper-arm cuff BP measurement was initiated approximately 2 s after each PPG recording. A curvature-based procedure identified pulse valleys, systolic peaks, dicrotic notches, and diastolic peaks, from which timing, amplitude, and amplitude ratio features were extracted. Separate linear regression models for systolic BP (SBP) and diastolic BP (DBP) were evaluated using participant-level ten-fold cross-validation. In each iteration, feature selection and model fitting were performed using only the nine training folds, and the fitted model was evaluated on the held-out fold. Results: In the descriptive analysis across all 48 participants, amplitude ratio features involving the systolic peak and dicrotic notch showed stronger associations with cuff-based BP readings than most individual timing and amplitude features. For green-light PPG, the systolic-peak-to-dicrotic-notch amplitude ratio (RatioSN) had a correlation of approximately 0.56 with SBP and 0.48 with DBP. Based on out-of-fold predictions, the best combined-feature models achieved root mean square errors of 12.87 mmHg for SBP and 7.17 mmHg for DBP, with corresponding R2 values of 0.87 and 0.83. Conclusions: Multi-wavelength PPG amplitude ratio features, particularly those involving the dicrotic notch, warrant further investigation for cuffless BP estimation. items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6872: MM-SleepNet: An Automatic Sleep Staging Network Based on Modal Re-Weighting and Mamba
items.summary: Sleep staging is the key step in sleep quality assessment and sleep disorder diagnosis. In clinical practice, doctors usually use polysomnography (PSG) to stage sleep. PSG contains physiological signals such as electroencephalography (EEG) and electrooculography (EOG) and is divided into continuous epochs of fixed duration. In order to achieve more efficient and accurate automatic interpretation of PSG, this paper proposes MM-SleepNet, an automatic sleep staging network based on modal re-weighting and Mamba. MM-SleepNet divides each epoch into several overlapping patches and uses a newly designed patch feature extractor to extract the features of each patch, in order to solve the problem of key waveforms in the patch being obscured by non-key waveforms throughout the epoch. Afterward, MM-SleepNet calculates the importance of different signals on patches at the same time point through a dynamic re-weighting module. MM-SleepNet uses a bidirectional Mamba encoder that considers positional encoding to learn contextual information across epochs to adapt to the transition patterns between sleep stages. The experimental results on the Sleep-EDF and ISRUC datasets show that the proposed MM-SleepNet outperforms state-of-the-art methods. In addition, ablation experiments have demonstrated the effectiveness of various modules in MM-SleepNet.

items.title: Evaluating Generalization and Long-Term Stability of Smartwatch-Based Cuffless Blood Pressure Monitoring
items.summary: Smartwatch-based cuffless blood pressure (BP) monitoring is a promising low-burden solution for long-term cardiovascular management, but practical deployment remains constrained by model complexity, uncertain cross-dataset generalization, and insufficient evidence on long-term tracking stability. This study presents an efficient Signal-Context Gated Fusion Network (SCGBPNet) for cuffless BP estimation from photoplethysmography (PPG) signals. SCGBPNet integrates signal-level representations through self-attention and further incorporates subject-specific contextual information via a compact gated fusion module. On Aurora-BP, SCGBPNet achieved SBP/DBP mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 7.08/4.90 mmHg, compared with 6.44/4.89 mmHg under within-dataset validation on the private smartwatch dataset, indicating a modest within-dataset discrepancy. Cross-dataset transfer from Aurora-BP to the smartwatch dataset increased the MAEs to 8.98/6.47 mmHg, demonstrating substantial cross-dataset degradation. For long-term stability, the proposed method showed low week-to-week performance variation and a low daily decay rate, indicating good stability over a follow-up period of more than one month. Nevertheless, estimation accuracy deteriorated when BP deviated substantially from an individual's baseline. These findings indicate that favorable aggregate MAE alone should not be interpreted as evidence of deployment-ready performance. More systematic and stratified evaluation across dataset settings, BP ranges, and baseline-deviation levels is needed to assess the practical reliability of smartwatch-based cuffless BP monitoring.

items.title: Wearable Biosensors for Early Detection and Continuous Monitoring of Postpartum Depression: A Human-Centered Approach
items.summary: Postpartum depression (PPD) is the leading cause of maternal mortality in the United States. However, there are significant gaps in PPD screening, detection, and treatment. A main challenge stems from limitations in existing methods for early PPD diagnosis and subsequent monitoring and intervention. Mobile technology that incorporates interactive interfaces and continuous wearable biosensors holds major potential to augment clinical decision-making and enhance PPD care. A number of compelling research directions exist in effectively developing such systems, including user experience design, sensing accuracy during perinatal stages, clinical integration and interoperability, acceptance and adoption, and privacy and ethics. By focusing on wearable devices that center women and their experiences, this paper discusses such challenges and opportunities at the intersections of HCI, inclusive physiological computing, and women's health.

items.title: ItemCompass: Real-Time Edge-AI Wearable Vision for Tag-Free Domestic Object Retrieval
items.summary: Misplacing household objects disrupts daily routines, especially for elderly users. ItemCompass addresses this with a real-time, tag-free wearable AR system that builds a persistent digital twin of the home for natural language object retrieval. A custom eyewear node streams visual and inertial data to an edge server, where YOLOv11n detection, Siamese re-identification, and a Pedestrian Dead Reckoning engine log object locations as Spatial Anchors in InfluxDB. Voice queries are resolved by a local Faster-Whisper and Qwen2 LLM pipeline, delivering concise spoken and AR guidance on a heads-up display. Evaluation shows 0.40 m localization drift, 97.5% step precision, and mAP@0.5 of 0.874, with users rating Accuracy and Trust at 4.6/5.0. The system highlights always-on sensing, conversational spatial memory, and privacy-by-design for wearable computing.

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6825: Vision-Floor Sensor Fusion for Non-Wearable Indoor Fall Detection Using Skeletal Motion and Distributed Force Sensing
items.summary: Falls represent a critical public health concern, particularly for older adults and individuals with disabilities, often resulting in serious injuries, loss of independence, and increased mortality. Traditional fall detection systems suffer from high false-positive rates, privacy concerns, and limited real-world applicability. This study presents an improved non-wearable fall detection method integrating YOLOv8-based skeletal pose estimation with load distribution sensing through decision-level sensor fusion. The system employs YOLOv8 for real-time human posture analysis and skeletal motion-based fall recognition, addressing limitations of simple presence-based or LiDAR-only approaches. A distributed load-sensing array embedded in the sensing surface monitors relative floor-loading patterns and impact-related changes. Decision-level fusion with temporal filtering combines skeletal postural and motion information with floor-load evidence, enabling accurate fall detection with substantially fewer false positives than the vision-only configuration. Key methodologies include detailed load sensor calibration, time-domain filtering to distinguish intentional lying from falls, and fusion logic leveraging the complementary strengths of visual and floor-based load sensing. Evaluation across 160 controlled trials involving eight healthy participants achieved an F1-score of 0.935, sensitivity of 90.0%, and specificity of 97.5%. Compared with the vision-only configuration, the fused framework reduced false-positive detections by 81.8%, although sensitivity decreased from 93.8% to 90.0%. This modular ROS2-based system provides a practical, non-intrusive framework with potential for future deployment in residential and assisted-living settings, while supporting extension to broader assistive monitoring applications.

items.title: An interoperable and reusable research environment for digital medicine
items.summary: Clinical research infrastructures remain fragmented and project-specific, with semantic inconsistency accumulating across studies and constantly increasing “interoperability debt”. Repeated transformations between heterogeneous standards cause semantic drift and information loss. Prospective studies require duplicate data entry across clinical and research systems, increasing workload and introducing inconsistencies. Project-driven data models accumulate technical debt that undermines the sustainability and maintainability of research infrastructure across studies and funding cycles. Here, we explore how a reusable research environment can be built, and whether governing data semantics at the persistence layer provides a foundation that outlasts individual projects. We present an environment addressing these deficiencies at the architectural level. An openEHR-based clinical data repository with governed archetypes serves as the canonical persistence layer, integrating retrospective EHR data, prospective study data, patient-reported outcomes, and wearable sensor streams under a shared semantic model. Prospective data is captured directly through openEHR-based forms, which removes the separate capture system for study variables, while duplicate documentation with a hospital information system that does not run on openEHR remains. Reusable transformation pipelines support bidirectional FHIR interoperability and OMOP-based analytics. Federation nodes at three institutions were tested with cohort count queries across sites and are not yet in routine use. Deployed at Charité university medical center across five studies covering approximately 16,000 patients and 7.9 million data points, the environment shows that one governed repository can be reused across successive studies from different clinical domains within an existing healthcare IT landscape. items.title: From continuous signals to accountable care: a trajectory-based framework for wearable monitoring in older adults
items.summary: Wearable technologies can continuously measure cardiovascular, physiological, and behavioral signals outside clinical settings, but more measurement does not necessarily produce better care. This limitation is particularly important in older adults, in whom frailty, multimorbidity, polypharmacy, cognitive impairment, altered vascular physiology, and caregiver dependence modify both signal reliability and clinical meaning. We argue that wearable monitoring in later life should move from population thresholds toward individualized physiological trajectories and from automated alerts toward accountable clinical action. We propose a trajectory-to-action framework based on five elements: individual baseline, within-person deviation, multimodal concordance, geriatric contextualization, and predefined clinical response. The framework is conceptual and has not been prospectively validated; its clinical utility, safety, implementation feasibility, and impact on outcomes require prospective testing. In this model, an alert is not a diagnosis but a request for attention whose recipient, response time, confirmatory pathway, and escalation rules are established in advance. Evaluation should therefore extend beyond sensor accuracy to include actionability, alert burden, clinical utility, equity, and net benefit. We propose that wearable monitoring in older adults should be evaluated by whether continuous signals can be translated into proportionate, context-aware, and accountable care.

items.title: Effectiveness of Wrist-Worn Wearable–Guided Cardiac Rehabilitation Delivered Through Fully Remote or Hybrid Programs in Patients With Cardiovascular Disease: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.summary: Background: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of death worldwide, yet participation in cardiac rehabilitation (CR) remains suboptimal. Wrist-worn wearables may support fully remote or hybrid CR through activity monitoring and individualized feedback, but the effectiveness and consistency of benefits remain uncertain. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of wrist-worn wearable–guided CR delivered through fully remote or hybrid programs initiated during phase II or III CR in patients with CVD. Methods: A total of 8 databases were searched for randomized controlled trials published from January 1, 2015, through August 7, 2026. Eligible trials enrolled adults with CVD and integrated a wrist-worn wearable into fully remote or hybrid CR. Studies focused primarily on heart failure or using wearables only for outcome measurement were excluded. Primary outcomes were peak oxygen consumption (VO 2 ), 6-minute walk distance (6MWD), and daily steps. Random-effects meta-analyses used mean differences (MDs), except for quality of life, which used standardized MDs. Between-study variance was estimated using the DerSimonian-Laird method, pooled-effect CIs used the Knapp-Hartung adjustment, and 95% prediction intervals (PIs) used the Nagashima-Noma-Furukawa parametric bootstrap method. Risk of bias was assessed with Cochrane Risk of Bias 2. Subgroup and univariable meta-regression analyses explored study and intervention characteristics. Results: A total of 18 trials involving 1993 randomized participants, reported in 20 publications, were included; 17 contributed to meta-analysis. Pooled estimates favored wearable-guided CR for peak VO 2 (10 studies; 591 participants; MD 1.69, 95% CI 0.46-2.92, 95% PI –2.21 to 5.39 mL/kg/min), 6MWD (9 studies; 1094 participants; MD 31.03, 95% CI 7.66-53.92, 95% PI –62.11 to 123.18 m), and daily steps (8 studies; 474 participants; MD 1062.8, 95% CI 383.5-1825.0, 95% PI –503.0 to 2860.0 steps/day). items.title: Robust PPG-Exclusive Heart Rate Estimation During Maximal Exercise Using Population-Based Priors
items.summary: PPG is the main technology for wearable heart rate (HR) monitoring. However, motion artifacts during intense physical activity reduce its reliability due to spectral overlap with the cardiac signal. This study investigates whether severely contaminated PPG signals can yield reliable HR estimates without auxiliary sensors by leveraging prior knowledge of HR dynamics. We acquired simultaneous PPG and ECG signals from 21 subjects during a maximal cycloergometer test. Using Leave-One-Subject-Out cross-validation, we built HR evolution priors from the ground-truth ECG and applied Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) to align normalized HR curves and estimate a barycenter average. DTW aligns normalized HR curves with minimal error across all subjects, validating robust population-based priors. For each test subject, we combined the PPG Power Spectral Density (PSD) with the prior distribution to generate a "posterior PSD". We identified and ranked candidate HR trajectories using heuristic search within the "posterior PSD" and selected the most likely path. Our approach reduced mean absolute error (MAE) in BPM relative to the ground-truth ECG by a median of 63.3% (IQR: 47.3%-74.6%) compared to a PPG+accelerometer benchmark. These results show that physiological priors and DTW-based alignment enable robust, PPG-exclusive HR monitoring during high-intensity exercise.

items.title: A Wearable Sensor Array on Conductive Textiles for Body Surface Temperature Mapping
items.summary: Continuous monitoring of body-surface temperature distributions can provide useful information for wearable health and thermal-condition monitoring. However, practical daily-use wearable systems for distributed temperature sensing remain difficult to implement because multiple sensor nodes require power delivery and data collection across a garment. Conventional wiring increases system complexity, reduces placement flexibility, and can compromise the wearability of garment-integrated sensor arrays. To address this issue, we present a conductive-textile-based wearable temperature sensing system in which the textile itself serves as a shared bus for both DC power delivery and data communication. Each sensor node is implemented as a compact, battery-free circular board with a diameter of 21 mm and a weight of 0.9 g, integrating a commercial temperature sensor and custom circuitry for UART/DC superposition. The shared textile bus enables flexible node placement without individual wiring while supplying power to each node. Address-based half-duplex UART with master polling enables collision-free multi-node communication. To demonstrate the system-level capability, we implemented an 18-node sensor array on a garment worn by a mannequin and developed a real-time temperature mapping viewer. In a thermal scanning demonstration using warm air from a heat gun with a set temperature of approximately 50 °C, the 18-node array captured spatiotemporal temperature variations over the garment surface at a refresh rate of 99.2 Hz. These results show that the proposed conductive-textile bus can support real-time, high-refresh-rate distributed temperature mapping, providing a practical basis for garment-integrated body-surface monitoring and future multi-sensor wearable systems.

items.title: MM-Net: A Multimodal Multi-Task Network for Sleep Staging and Sleep Apnea Assessment After Ischemic Stroke
items.summary: Automated polysomnography after ischemic stroke is challenging because of altered sleep-related neural activity and concurrent respiratory disturbances. Existing stroke-specific approaches mainly address sleep-stage classification, leaving joint analysis of sleep architecture and respiratory events underexplored. Moreover, adapting pretrained EEG encoders introduces a representation inconsistency when downstream models are trained on embeddings from previously seen patients but evaluated on unseen individuals. We propose MM-Net, a multimodal multi-task framework that resolves this inconsistency through cross-fitting and ridge-based embedding alignment. Sleep-adapted EEG-EOG representations and engineered neural descriptors are fused with learned cardiorespiratory features through cross-attention and shared temporal modeling for simultaneous sleep staging and respiratory-event detection. On iSLEEPS (99 patients with subacute ischemic stroke), ten-fold patient-independent evaluation achieved 76.3% staging accuracy (Cohen's $κ$ = 0.656) and 0.825 respiratory-event AUC, outperforming the evaluated baselines under matched protocols. The sleep-adapted encoder improved the downstream model when its embeddings were aligned, raising staging accuracy by 1.4 percentage points over the frozen encoder ($p$ = 0.020) versus 0.2 points without alignment. MM-Net also achieved 86.4% staging accuracy on Sleep-EDF, above every single-EEG architecture reimplemented on the same recordings, and 80.3% staging accuracy with 0.889 respiratory AUC on ISRUC-I, exceeding its retrained staging baselines. Without retraining, the iSLEEPS-trained model retained respiratory AUCs of 0.833 on ISRUC-I and 0.841 on UCD. These findings support representation-consistent neural adaptation and joint physiological modeling across stroke, healthy-sleep, and sleep-disorder cohorts.

items.title: The Metrology Atlas: describing recorded physiological data as a measurement system, with VitalDB as a first application
items.summary: Every value in a recorded physiological dataset is a pair: a recorded time and a recorded value. Neither is the truth. The time comes from a clock that drifts and is corrected in jumps, and often describes a window that ended earlier. The value was quantised, rounded, sometimes heaped by hand, and measured by an instrument with its own error. We present the Metrology Atlas, a dataset-independent way of describing a recorded dataset as a measurement system, and its first application, to VitalDB, an open dataset of 6,388 surgical patients, as a proof of principle. For every variable, the atlas states what was measured, the measurement model linking it to the recorded pair, and what is known about the true time and true value given a record. Each part of the model carries its evidence: 69 studies, 49 parameters and 54 observations, each marked as measured, derived, estimated or assumed. The atlas maps 11 clocks and 14 devices into one timing network, and closes loops in that network to test its own model. Synchronisation reduces the median timing error between the EEG and ECG from 794 ms to 42 ms, and between ventilator and monitor waveforms from 378 ms to 55 ms. The atlas also documents data-quality issues, several of which correct the dataset's own documentation. It is published as a website and a single machine-readable file, with open-source code and a scheme of time-aware labels. Everything is open under CC BY 4.0 and MIT licences. The engine, schema and timing tools carry over unchanged, and the aim is to describe many other datasets the same way.

items.title: Interaction-Gated Time-Frequency Learning for Parameter-Efficient PPG-Based Heart Rate Estimation
items.summary: Photoplethysmography (PPG) enables low-cost and non-invasive heart rate (HR) monitoring but remains sensitive to waveform distortion, physiological variability, and measurement interference. Temporal waveform characteristics and frequency-domain periodicity provide complementary information for HR estimation; however, effectively exploring and integrating these representations within a compact model remains challenging. This paper proposes TF-IG, a parameter-efficient interaction-gated time-frequency learning framework for PPG-based HR estimation. TF-IG employs a dual-branch architecture in which a temporal branch captures pulse morphology via dilated depthwise-separable convolutions, while a frequency branch extracts cardiac periodicity information from bounded log-spectrogram representations. To combine the two domains, we introduce an interaction-gated fusion module that explicitly models feature agreement and discrepancy, while also learning feature-wise weights to balance temporal and spectral information. A parameter-shared regression head further maps the temporal, spectral, and fused representations into the final HR prediction space. Experiments on the benchmark BIDMC PPG and Respiration Dataset using a subject-exclusive training, validation, and test protocol show that TF-IG achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.227 BPM, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 2.060 BPM, a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.9934, and 92.28 percent of estimates within 3 BPM, while remaining parameter-efficient with only 84.6K parameters. Ablation results further demonstrate the complementary contributions of the temporal and frequency branches, interaction-gated fusion, and shared regression head. These results indicate that explicitly modeling cross-domain interactions provides an effective accuracy-complexity trade-off for lightweight PPG-based HR estimation.

items.title: ECG-SDI: Single-lead Electrocardiogram Enables Continuous Sleep Depth Index Profiling and Scalable Digital Biomarkers for Sleep Health
items.summary: Conventional sleep staging provides a coarse-grained representation that obscures within-stage depth variation. We developed ECG-SDI, a single-lead electrocardiography (ECG) framework for continuous sleep-depth profiling and digital biomarker extraction. Using 12,392 overnight polysomnographic recordings, we trained and validated a two-stage deep learning model supervised by conventional sleep-stage labels. Correlations with ordered stages excluding rapid eye movement (REM) sleep were 0.828 in the pooled internal test set and 0.848 in the external Cleveland Family Study; corresponding REM classification AUROCs were 0.954 and 0.977. Overnight trajectories captured within-stage variation. Biomarker-based phenotyping identified a disturbed subtype associated with poorer subjective sleep quality and higher all-cause mortality in the Sleep Heart Health Study (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.20; 95% CI, 1.05-1.38). Among 507 participants with paired recordings before and after continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), normalized sleep-depth area increased by 6.1% and shallow-sleep burden below 0.3 decreased by 16.0%. Exploratory analyses linked reductions in approximate entropy and depth variability to reduced oxygen desaturation and increased sleep efficiency, respectively (Spearman rho = 0.24 and 0.12); both associations remained positive after covariate adjustment. Mean ECG-SDI within N2 increased by 0.017 (95% CI, 0.004-0.030). A wearable proof-of-concept illustrated the acquisition-to-report workflow. These findings support ECG-based sleep phenotyping and further evaluation of CPAP response monitoring at home.

items.title: Contactless gait-derived features as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity in adolescents
items.summary: Timely assessment of depression severity in adolescents is essential for guiding clinical care, yet conventional evaluations rely on episodic clinical assessments and symptom rating scales. Contactless gait analysis offers a potentially scalable approach to capturing objective behavioral features associated with depression. Here, we introduce the Long-Distance 3D Adolescent Depression Gait Dataset (LD3D-ADG), comprising depth-sensor gait recordings from 119 adolescents at a single center, including 39 healthy controls, 41 with mild depression, and 39 with moderate-to-severe depression. We developed UMLPA-GCN, a graph convolutional network that models spatiotemporal gait dynamics across three anatomically defined skeletal partitions. In participant-independent five-fold cross-validation, UMLPA-GCN achieved 75.63% classification accuracy, a macro-F1 score of 75.52%, and a macro-area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.839 (95% confidence interval, 0.779--0.899). Class-specific recall was 87.18%, 63.41%, and 76.92% for healthy controls, mild depression, and moderate-to-severe depression, respectively. At the participant level, reduced arm swing, slower pelvic movement, restricted joint range of motion, and greater arm-swing asymmetry were identified as leading potential digital biomarkers contributing to depression severity assessment, associated with higher 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores. These findings provide proof-of-concept evidence for contactless digital depression severity stratification in adolescents. Further external and prospective validation is needed to establish their utility for longitudinal monitoring and timely clinical assessment.

items.title: Task-evoked eye movements as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity in adolescents and young adults
items.summary: Objective digital measures of depression severity could complement conventional symptom assessments and facilitate more timely clinical evaluation. Here, we investigated whether task-evoked eye movements provide interpretable behavioral markers of depression severity in adolescents and young adults. In this single-center, cross-sectional study, 155 participants aged 14--20 years completed emotional-spatial free-viewing and memory-guided recall tasks and were stratified by 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores. We examined 19 prespecified eye-movement features across six task-informed domains using covariate-adjusted ordinal-trend models. Greater depression severity was associated with lower gaze-allocation entropy (standardized $β=-0.599$), fewer inter-area switches ($β=-0.526$), longer first target-entry latency ($β=0.572$), and lower target dwell proportion ($β=-0.678$; all false-discovery-rate-adjusted $q<0.001$). Emotion-specific attentional-bias measures were not associated with severity, whereas associations involving fixation dispersion weakened after adjustment for anxiety symptoms. In a complementary machine-learning analysis incorporating 44 candidate eye-movement features and demographic covariates, a three-stage cascade classifier achieved the highest four-class stratification performance (accuracy, 0.665; macro-F1, 0.670; area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, 0.869), outperforming single-stage and two-stage approaches. Together, these findings identify altered visual exploration and memory-guided gaze control as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity, rather than generalized negative attentional bias. These results support further prospective evaluation of task-evoked eye tracking as a complementary approach for timely severity assessment and clinical decision support.

items.title: FALLNEST: Dual-Domain Dataset Condensation of Imbalanced IMU Data for Wearable Fall Detection
items.summary: Wearable fall detection is hampered by rare fall events, scarce labeled IMU data, and the cost of training deep models on large, imbalanced corpora. Existing methods either rely on hand-crafted features with shallow classifiers, which limits learning from raw signals, or train deep networks on full datasets that require re-sampling to counter class skew and demand substantial data and compute. To address this, we propose a novel Fall detection framework via Normalized-gradient and Embedding matched Synthetic Time-frequency condensation, dubbed FALLNEST, a data-centric approach that distills large, imbalanced IMU datasets into tiny, class-balanced synthetic training sets. Building on dual-domain time-series condensation (CondTSC), FALLNEST introduces a fall-specific 7-channel input with accelerometer vector magnitude, class-balanced K-Means initialization, and normalized gradient matching with gradient clipping, combined with MMD-based embedding alignment and multi-view Fourier-domain augmentation, so that class balance arises from the condensed set itself rather than from re-sampling. We evaluate on SisFall, KFall, and MobiFall using strict subject-wise splits and naturally imbalanced test sets, reporting accuracy, Macro-F1, and PR-AUC over five seeds. A 102K-parameter TinyCNN trained on only 32 to 146 synthetic windows (about only 1% of the training windows) reaches 93.5-95.8% mean accuracy and 0.89-0.98 PR-AUC, with standard deviations of 1.0-1.7% in accuracy, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach.

items.title: ECG-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Targeted Electrocardiogram Waveform Evolution
items.summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) models need supervision that targets evolving weaknesses and remains faithful to waveform evidence. We introduce ECG-RSI, a recursive self-improvement framework combining verified waveform synthesis with feedback-guided intervention search. Signal remeasurement verifies waveform edits; construction errors guide generator repair, while learner errors motivate interventions compared on a separate selection set. Across seven benchmarks, three rounds raise Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's mean question-answering accuracy from 34.57% to 56.04% and mean classification F1 from 24.27 to 34.03. Across the retained trajectory, the preferred supervision shifts from direct reinforcement to confusion-focused contrasts. Continued feedback correction yields diminishing external gains. These results motivate separating error diagnosis from intervention selection and checking whether gains on the feedback set transfer to independent benchmarks.

items.title: A Co-Located MMG-FES Wearable Interface for Action-Updated State-Gated Stimulation
items.summary: Functional electrical stimulation (FES) assists movement, but fixed schedules cannot track how a repeatedly activated muscle changes, and surface electromyography (EMG) near the stimulation electrodes is often obscured by artifacts. Prior work recorded mechanomyography (MMG) passively during closed-loop FES cycling and estimated FES-induced fatigue or predicted fatigue for FES control, without gating stimulation with stimulated-site MMG. In this study, we present VG-FES, a wearable module co-locating microphone-based MMG, programmable charge-balanced biphasic stimulation, and embedded state-gated control at one on-skin thigh site. After each action, we compare rectus femoris (RF) mean power frequency (MPF) with an early-session baseline of the same direction, giving a relative state. A threshold on its window means enables fixed-duration bursts separated by rest periods. During onboard stimulation, MMG remained recordable, whereas near-site EMG was artifact-dominated. Under prolonged external stimulation, cycle-wise MMG tracked an independent local-pressure reference (Spearman rho = 0.968). In leave-one-session-out evaluation on 2284 squat actions (11 sessions, eight participants), MMG-based action segmentation reached an event-detection F1 of 0.923 and direction classification a balanced accuracy of 0.925. Online, over 15.69 min of self-paced squats, one participant received four bursts while MMG acquisition and action monitoring continued. Mechanical feedback from the stimulated site offers wearable FES and assistive robotics a per-action basis for state-gated stimulation.

items.title: ECGWmark: Deep Watermarking of Electrocardiogram Signals With Error-Correcting Codes
items.summary: Wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings pass through multiple networks and systems before automated interpretation, making patient metadata vulnerable to loss. Digital watermarking embeds this metadata directly into the signal. However, conventional ECG watermarking methods fail under temporal desynchronization, and waveform similarity does not guarantee downstream diagnostic preservation. This article presents ECGWmark, a deep watermarking framework for single-lead ECG. A fully convolutional generator embeds the payload without signal quantization, a detector decodes the message frame by frame and verifies watermark presence, and a frozen arrhythmia classifier penalizes changes that would alter diagnostic predictions. To bridge the gap between bit accuracy and whole-message recovery, payloads are protected by extended Hamming codes, validation-selected interleaving, and soft-decision decoding. On the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, ECGWmark maintains over 90\% bit accuracy under time shifts of 10 to 50 samples, where transform baselines fall to chance level. With the coding layer, the protected 16-bit payload achieves 99.86\% exact recovery on clean segments and sustains over 90\% recovery under time shifts, 10\% sample deletion, and 10\% packet loss. Inter-patient evaluation confirms improved ventricular-beat sensitivity with preserved macro-F1. Requiring only 0.56 million parameters and about 15ms per segment on a desktop CPU, ECGWmark highlights the need to assess physiological watermarking through whole-message recovery and diagnostic consistency.

items.title: A Group-Aware Comparative Study of Classical Machine Learning and Deep Learning Methods for Sensor-Based Human Activity Recognition
items.summary: Human Activity Recognition (HAR) using wearable or smartphone inertial sensors is commonly evaluated with both classical machine learning and deep learning methods. However, reported performance can be strongly affected by sensor modality, dataset characteristics, and data-splitting strategy. This study presents a controlled comparative evaluation of four classical machine learning models and four deep learning models on two public HAR datasets, UCI-HAR and KU-HAR. Three sensor modalities were considered: accelerometer (ACC), gyroscope (GYRO), and their combination (ACC+GYRO). Classical machine learning models used handcrafted statistical features, while deep learning models operated directly on raw sensor sequences. The primary evaluation employed five-fold StratifiedGroupKFold cross-validation, with subject- or participant-level grouping to prevent group overlap between training and test folds. Macro-F1 was used as the primary performance metric. The results show that deep learning did not consistently outperform classical machine learning. On UCI-HAR, the evaluated deep learning models achieved slightly higher macro-F1 values, whereas on KU-HAR, LightGBM achieved 0.857 compared with 0.828 for the highest-performing evaluated deep learning model. Regarding sensor modality, the combined ACC+GYRO configuration generally outperformed ACC or GYRO alone on both datasets. The evaluation protocol also had a substantial effect: for CNNBiLSTMAttn with ACC+GYRO, random splitting increased macro-F1 by 0.033 on UCI-HAR and 0.093 on KU-HAR compared with grouped evaluation. These findings highlight the importance of model family, sensor modality, dataset characteristics, and group-aware evaluation when assessing sensor-based HAR systems.

items.title: AI-Driven Urge Regulation Assistant (AURA): Designing Preemptive Smart Wearables for Smoking Cessation
items.summary: Smoking cessation remains a complex self-regulatory challenge, often undermined by cue-triggered cravings arising from habitual, emotional, and social contexts. Existing wearable cessation systems are largely reactive, detecting smoking events only after lapses occur and thus missing the critical window for timely intervention. Guided by cue-reactivity theory and Self-Determination Theory (SDT), we argue that future digital health systems should shift from retrospective feedback toward proactive craving management that supports user autonomy and competence. To inform the design of such systems, we present a formative pilot qualitative study involving semi-structured interviews with 10 smokers and ex-smokers from a multi-ethnic Asian population, a demographic underrepresented in current wearable AI and smoking cessation research. Through an iterative co-design interview process, we examine (1) the barriers and facilitators to smoking cessation and (2) the desired design features of wearable systems targeting cravings before lapses occur. Our findings identify key craving predictors across habitual, emotional, and social dimensions, alongside user-preferred intervention strategies such as social accountability, personalized support, rewards, and just-in-time distraction techniques. Participants also emphasized the importance of trust, privacy, personalization, and non-judgmental interaction styles. These insights directly inform the design of AURA, a novel smartwatch-smartphone ecosystem for proactive craving detection and intervention using commercially available wearable devices.

items.title: BeatFlow-ECG: Rectified Flow for ECG Reconstruction from Indirect Wearable Signals
items.summary: Continuous cardiac monitoring outside clinical settings requires signals that are both informative and practical to collect during daily life. Electrocardiography (ECG) provides rich information about cardiac rhythm and waveform morphology, while wearable photoplethysmography (PPG) is easier to acquire continuously but is only an indirect cardiovascular measurement and is highly sensitive to motion. We present BeatFlow-ECG, a conditional rectified-flow model for reconstructing single-channel ECG from synchronized PPG and inertial measurements. BeatFlow-ECG models reconstruction as conditional transport from noise to ECG using a convolutional encoder-decoder with a transformer bottleneck and explicit flow-time conditioning. Motion information is incorporated through IMU-derived conditioning features, motion-dependent loss weighting, and an easy-to-hard training curriculum. We evaluate the model under leave-one-subject-out protocols on PPG-DaLiA and WESAD. BeatFlow-ECG achieves the best results among the evaluated deterministic, adversarial, and diffusion-based baselines across all reported waveform and beat-timing metrics, with Pearson correlations of 0.983 and 0.986 and R-peak F1 scores of 0.946 and 0.955, respectively. Compared with Conditional DDPM-1D, L1 error decreases from 0.085 to 0.062 on PPG-DaLiA and from 0.074 to 0.055 on WESAD. Additional analyses on PPG-DaLiA show higher correlation in fixed R-peak-relative waveform regions and lower reconstruction error across low-, medium-, and high-motion subsets.

items.title: REFIT: Recognize, Fix, and Test Wearable Sensor Placement Shifts without Labels
items.summary: We present REFIT, an input calibration for frozen activity-recognition models whose inertial sensors are worn differently at deployment than in training. When users move a watch to the other wrist or put a strap sensor back on turned, the model sees the same motion on changed axes. REFIT undoes such shifts without labels or retraining. It describes them by families of axis transforms, such as reflections and rotations, and fits each family to the user's data so that simple statistics match those of the training data. The family that removes most of the mismatch names the shift. REFIT fixes the shift by applying the best member of that family before the frozen model and re-estimating its normalization statistics. It tests the fixed model with a label-free accuracy estimate and asks the user to re-wear the sensor when it is low. Experiments on real left/right sensor pairs and on real and simulated re-attachment show that REFIT outperforms label-free test-time adaptation methods on every dataset and restores most of the accuracy lost to re-attachment. It names injected shifts far more reliably than a confidence-based selector. After a correction over all signed permutations of the axes, the estimate separates successful from failed corrections.

items.title: Label-Efficient Deep Learning for ECG Delineation: A Multi-Dataset Benchmark against Widely Used Delineation Tools
items.summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) delineation, the identification of waveform boundaries, is a foundational step that translates raw ECG signals into clinically interpretable measurements. Deep learning has advanced this task but remains dependent on costly expert annotations. Label-efficient strategies such as self-supervised pretraining and semi-supervised learning are expected to ease this burden, yet it remains unclear whether they yield reliable delineation and whether the deep models they produce outperform the delineation tools used in practice. We address this in two stages. First, comparing self-supervised objectives with supervised or semi-supervised fine-tuning across one internal and four external datasets, we find that pretraining helps but the objective matters, and that the value of semi-supervised fine-tuning depends on the pretraining objective. Second, we benchmark the selected deep learning model against widely used open-source (NeuroKit2, Prominence, ECGdeli) and commercial (CalECG) tools using three complementary metrics. The model ranks best on every metric and dataset, outperforming the strongest tool by a clear margin on the rhythm-diverse set (mIoU 71.3 vs. 54.8%; averaged point-wise sensitivity 92.6 vs. 76.4%), and degrades the least from sinus to arrhythmia. A rhythm-stratified and point-wise analysis further characterizes the distinctive behavior of each tool, yielding practical guidance for tool selection. These results provide systematic, multi-dataset evidence that self-supervised pretraining is effective for ECG delineation and enables a label-efficiently trained deep learning model to outperform widely used delineation tools by leveraging abundant unlabeled data. This supports adopting such models in diverse, real-world clinical settings.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6912: Improving Wearable PPG Monitoring with Morphology-Aware and Learning-Driven Heartbeat Detection
academic.summary: Photoplethysmography (PPG) is a widely used, non-invasive technique for heart rate monitoring, but its reliability is often compromised by noise and motion artifacts (MAs). This study presents the Peakwise Correlation Pulse Detector (PCPD), an algorithm for detecting heartbeats directly from PPG signals without requiring electrocardiogram (ECG) signals during operation, evaluated here under clean and controlled synthetic pulse-free-noise conditions. PCPD follows a five-step pipeline: (1) signal segmentation with overlap, (2) sliding cross-correlation using high-quality heartbeat templates, (3) computation of the Minimum Correlation Curve (MCC), (4) feature extraction with machine learning-based classification, and (5) peak translation with constraint analysis. The method was evaluated on a clean dataset, comprising a newly collected PPG dataset with manually annotated signal quality and the publicly available BIDMC dataset, and on a noisy dataset that augments the clean data with synthetic pulse-free segments generated from band-limited Gaussian noise. This evaluation framework tests heartbeat detectors under ideal conditions and under a controlled non-informative-noise protocol. On clean signals, PCPD achieved balanced precision-recall scores of 99.13% on the proposed dataset (internal performance) and 97.04% on the independent BIDMC dataset. Under added synthetic pulse-free noise, PCPD achieved accuracies of 99.30% and 97.16% on the proposed and BIDMC datasets, respectively. In comparative experiments against eleven benchmark heartbeat detection algorithms, PCPD achieved the best performance among the evaluated implementations under the tested synthetic-noise protocol. These results support PCPD as a promising PPG-only peak detector and motivate further validation under real motion artifacts and for downstream signal quality assessment.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6897: Multi-Wavelength PPG Amplitude Ratio Features for Cuffless Blood Pressure Estimation: An Exploratory Study
academic.summary: Background: Cuffless blood pressure (BP) estimation from photoplethysmography (PPG) remains challenging. This exploratory study investigated whether curvature-derived waveform features from multiple PPG wavelengths, particularly amplitude ratios, are associated with cuff-based BP readings. Methods: Red, infrared, and green PPG signals were recorded for 90 s from 48 physician-screened volunteers (23 males and 25 females; mean age, 63.41 +/- 14.20 years). A single automated upper-arm cuff BP measurement was initiated approximately 2 s after each PPG recording. A curvature-based procedure identified pulse valleys, systolic peaks, dicrotic notches, and diastolic peaks, from which timing, amplitude, and amplitude ratio features were extracted. Separate linear regression models for systolic BP (SBP) and diastolic BP (DBP) were evaluated using participant-level ten-fold cross-validation. In each iteration, feature selection and model fitting were performed using only the nine training folds, and the fitted model was evaluated on the held-out fold. Results: In the descriptive analysis across all 48 participants, amplitude ratio features involving the systolic peak and dicrotic notch showed stronger associations with cuff-based BP readings than most individual timing and amplitude features. For green-light PPG, the systolic-peak-to-dicrotic-notch amplitude ratio (RatioSN) had a correlation of approximately 0.56 with SBP and 0.48 with DBP. Based on out-of-fold predictions, the best combined-feature models achieved root mean square errors of 12.87 mmHg for SBP and 7.17 mmHg for DBP, with corresponding R2 values of 0.87 and 0.83. Conclusions: Multi-wavelength PPG amplitude ratio features, particularly those involving the dicrotic notch, warrant further investigation for cuffless BP estimation. academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6872: MM-SleepNet: An Automatic Sleep Staging Network Based on Modal Re-Weighting and Mamba
academic.summary: Sleep staging is the key step in sleep quality assessment and sleep disorder diagnosis. In clinical practice, doctors usually use polysomnography (PSG) to stage sleep. PSG contains physiological signals such as electroencephalography (EEG) and electrooculography (EOG) and is divided into continuous epochs of fixed duration. In order to achieve more efficient and accurate automatic interpretation of PSG, this paper proposes MM-SleepNet, an automatic sleep staging network based on modal re-weighting and Mamba. MM-SleepNet divides each epoch into several overlapping patches and uses a newly designed patch feature extractor to extract the features of each patch, in order to solve the problem of key waveforms in the patch being obscured by non-key waveforms throughout the epoch. Afterward, MM-SleepNet calculates the importance of different signals on patches at the same time point through a dynamic re-weighting module. MM-SleepNet uses a bidirectional Mamba encoder that considers positional encoding to learn contextual information across epochs to adapt to the transition patterns between sleep stages. The experimental results on the Sleep-EDF and ISRUC datasets show that the proposed MM-SleepNet outperforms state-of-the-art methods. In addition, ablation experiments have demonstrated the effectiveness of various modules in MM-SleepNet.

academic.title: Evaluating Generalization and Long-Term Stability of Smartwatch-Based Cuffless Blood Pressure Monitoring
academic.summary: Smartwatch-based cuffless blood pressure (BP) monitoring is a promising low-burden solution for long-term cardiovascular management, but practical deployment remains constrained by model complexity, uncertain cross-dataset generalization, and insufficient evidence on long-term tracking stability. This study presents an efficient Signal-Context Gated Fusion Network (SCGBPNet) for cuffless BP estimation from photoplethysmography (PPG) signals. SCGBPNet integrates signal-level representations through self-attention and further incorporates subject-specific contextual information via a compact gated fusion module. On Aurora-BP, SCGBPNet achieved SBP/DBP mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 7.08/4.90 mmHg, compared with 6.44/4.89 mmHg under within-dataset validation on the private smartwatch dataset, indicating a modest within-dataset discrepancy. Cross-dataset transfer from Aurora-BP to the smartwatch dataset increased the MAEs to 8.98/6.47 mmHg, demonstrating substantial cross-dataset degradation. For long-term stability, the proposed method showed low week-to-week performance variation and a low daily decay rate, indicating good stability over a follow-up period of more than one month. Nevertheless, estimation accuracy deteriorated when BP deviated substantially from an individual's baseline. These findings indicate that favorable aggregate MAE alone should not be interpreted as evidence of deployment-ready performance. More systematic and stratified evaluation across dataset settings, BP ranges, and baseline-deviation levels is needed to assess the practical reliability of smartwatch-based cuffless BP monitoring.

academic.title: Wearable Biosensors for Early Detection and Continuous Monitoring of Postpartum Depression: A Human-Centered Approach
academic.summary: Postpartum depression (PPD) is the leading cause of maternal mortality in the United States. However, there are significant gaps in PPD screening, detection, and treatment. A main challenge stems from limitations in existing methods for early PPD diagnosis and subsequent monitoring and intervention. Mobile technology that incorporates interactive interfaces and continuous wearable biosensors holds major potential to augment clinical decision-making and enhance PPD care. A number of compelling research directions exist in effectively developing such systems, including user experience design, sensing accuracy during perinatal stages, clinical integration and interoperability, acceptance and adoption, and privacy and ethics. By focusing on wearable devices that center women and their experiences, this paper discusses such challenges and opportunities at the intersections of HCI, inclusive physiological computing, and women's health.

academic.title: ItemCompass: Real-Time Edge-AI Wearable Vision for Tag-Free Domestic Object Retrieval
academic.summary: Misplacing household objects disrupts daily routines, especially for elderly users. ItemCompass addresses this with a real-time, tag-free wearable AR system that builds a persistent digital twin of the home for natural language object retrieval. A custom eyewear node streams visual and inertial data to an edge server, where YOLOv11n detection, Siamese re-identification, and a Pedestrian Dead Reckoning engine log object locations as Spatial Anchors in InfluxDB. Voice queries are resolved by a local Faster-Whisper and Qwen2 LLM pipeline, delivering concise spoken and AR guidance on a heads-up display. Evaluation shows 0.40 m localization drift, 97.5% step precision, and mAP@0.5 of 0.874, with users rating Accuracy and Trust at 4.6/5.0. The system highlights always-on sensing, conversational spatial memory, and privacy-by-design for wearable computing.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6825: Vision-Floor Sensor Fusion for Non-Wearable Indoor Fall Detection Using Skeletal Motion and Distributed Force Sensing
academic.summary: Falls represent a critical public health concern, particularly for older adults and individuals with disabilities, often resulting in serious injuries, loss of independence, and increased mortality. Traditional fall detection systems suffer from high false-positive rates, privacy concerns, and limited real-world applicability. This study presents an improved non-wearable fall detection method integrating YOLOv8-based skeletal pose estimation with load distribution sensing through decision-level sensor fusion. The system employs YOLOv8 for real-time human posture analysis and skeletal motion-based fall recognition, addressing limitations of simple presence-based or LiDAR-only approaches. A distributed load-sensing array embedded in the sensing surface monitors relative floor-loading patterns and impact-related changes. Decision-level fusion with temporal filtering combines skeletal postural and motion information with floor-load evidence, enabling accurate fall detection with substantially fewer false positives than the vision-only configuration. Key methodologies include detailed load sensor calibration, time-domain filtering to distinguish intentional lying from falls, and fusion logic leveraging the complementary strengths of visual and floor-based load sensing. Evaluation across 160 controlled trials involving eight healthy participants achieved an F1-score of 0.935, sensitivity of 90.0%, and specificity of 97.5%. Compared with the vision-only configuration, the fused framework reduced false-positive detections by 81.8%, although sensitivity decreased from 93.8% to 90.0%. This modular ROS2-based system provides a practical, non-intrusive framework with potential for future deployment in residential and assisted-living settings, while supporting extension to broader assistive monitoring applications.

academic.title: An interoperable and reusable research environment for digital medicine
academic.summary: Clinical research infrastructures remain fragmented and project-specific, with semantic inconsistency accumulating across studies and constantly increasing “interoperability debt”. Repeated transformations between heterogeneous standards cause semantic drift and information loss. Prospective studies require duplicate data entry across clinical and research systems, increasing workload and introducing inconsistencies. Project-driven data models accumulate technical debt that undermines the sustainability and maintainability of research infrastructure across studies and funding cycles. Here, we explore how a reusable research environment can be built, and whether governing data semantics at the persistence layer provides a foundation that outlasts individual projects. We present an environment addressing these deficiencies at the architectural level. An openEHR-based clinical data repository with governed archetypes serves as the canonical persistence layer, integrating retrospective EHR data, prospective study data, patient-reported outcomes, and wearable sensor streams under a shared semantic model. Prospective data is captured directly through openEHR-based forms, which removes the separate capture system for study variables, while duplicate documentation with a hospital information system that does not run on openEHR remains. Reusable transformation pipelines support bidirectional FHIR interoperability and OMOP-based analytics. Federation nodes at three institutions were tested with cohort count queries across sites and are not yet in routine use. Deployed at Charité university medical center across five studies covering approximately 16,000 patients and 7.9 million data points, the environment shows that one governed repository can be reused across successive studies from different clinical domains within an existing healthcare IT landscape. academic.title: From continuous signals to accountable care: a trajectory-based framework for wearable monitoring in older adults
academic.summary: Wearable technologies can continuously measure cardiovascular, physiological, and behavioral signals outside clinical settings, but more measurement does not necessarily produce better care. This limitation is particularly important in older adults, in whom frailty, multimorbidity, polypharmacy, cognitive impairment, altered vascular physiology, and caregiver dependence modify both signal reliability and clinical meaning. We argue that wearable monitoring in later life should move from population thresholds toward individualized physiological trajectories and from automated alerts toward accountable clinical action. We propose a trajectory-to-action framework based on five elements: individual baseline, within-person deviation, multimodal concordance, geriatric contextualization, and predefined clinical response. The framework is conceptual and has not been prospectively validated; its clinical utility, safety, implementation feasibility, and impact on outcomes require prospective testing. In this model, an alert is not a diagnosis but a request for attention whose recipient, response time, confirmatory pathway, and escalation rules are established in advance. Evaluation should therefore extend beyond sensor accuracy to include actionability, alert burden, clinical utility, equity, and net benefit. We propose that wearable monitoring in older adults should be evaluated by whether continuous signals can be translated into proportionate, context-aware, and accountable care.

academic.summary: Background: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of death worldwide, yet participation in cardiac rehabilitation (CR) remains suboptimal. Wrist-worn wearables may support fully remote or hybrid CR through activity monitoring and individualized feedback, but the effectiveness and consistency of benefits remain uncertain. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of wrist-worn wearable–guided CR delivered through fully remote or hybrid programs initiated during phase II or III CR in patients with CVD. Risk of bias was assessed with Cochrane Risk of Bias 2. Subgroup and univariable meta-regression analyses explored study and intervention characteristics. academic.title: Robust PPG-Exclusive Heart Rate Estimation During Maximal Exercise Using Population-Based Priors
academic.summary: PPG is the main technology for wearable heart rate (HR) monitoring. However, motion artifacts during intense physical activity reduce its reliability due to spectral overlap with the cardiac signal. This study investigates whether severely contaminated PPG signals can yield reliable HR estimates without auxiliary sensors by leveraging prior knowledge of HR dynamics. We acquired simultaneous PPG and ECG signals from 21 subjects during a maximal cycloergometer test. Using Leave-One-Subject-Out cross-validation, we built HR evolution priors from the ground-truth ECG and applied Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) to align normalized HR curves and estimate a barycenter average. DTW aligns normalized HR curves with minimal error across all subjects, validating robust population-based priors. For each test subject, we combined the PPG Power Spectral Density (PSD) with the prior distribution to generate a "posterior PSD". We identified and ranked candidate HR trajectories using heuristic search within the "posterior PSD" and selected the most likely path. Our approach reduced mean absolute error (MAE) in BPM relative to the ground-truth ECG by a median of 63.3% (IQR: 47.3%-74.6%) compared to a PPG+accelerometer benchmark. These results show that physiological priors and DTW-based alignment enable robust, PPG-exclusive HR monitoring during high-intensity exercise.

academic.title: A Wearable Sensor Array on Conductive Textiles for Body Surface Temperature Mapping
academic.summary: Continuous monitoring of body-surface temperature distributions can provide useful information for wearable health and thermal-condition monitoring. However, practical daily-use wearable systems for distributed temperature sensing remain difficult to implement because multiple sensor nodes require power delivery and data collection across a garment. Conventional wiring increases system complexity, reduces placement flexibility, and can compromise the wearability of garment-integrated sensor arrays. To address this issue, we present a conductive-textile-based wearable temperature sensing system in which the textile itself serves as a shared bus for both DC power delivery and data communication. Each sensor node is implemented as a compact, battery-free circular board with a diameter of 21 mm and a weight of 0.9 g, integrating a commercial temperature sensor and custom circuitry for UART/DC superposition. The shared textile bus enables flexible node placement without individual wiring while supplying power to each node. Address-based half-duplex UART with master polling enables collision-free multi-node communication. To demonstrate the system-level capability, we implemented an 18-node sensor array on a garment worn by a mannequin and developed a real-time temperature mapping viewer. In a thermal scanning demonstration using warm air from a heat gun with a set temperature of approximately 50 °C, the 18-node array captured spatiotemporal temperature variations over the garment surface at a refresh rate of 99.2 Hz. These results show that the proposed conductive-textile bus can support real-time, high-refresh-rate distributed temperature mapping, providing a practical basis for garment-integrated body-surface monitoring and future multi-sensor wearable systems.

academic.title: MM-Net: A Multimodal Multi-Task Network for Sleep Staging and Sleep Apnea Assessment After Ischemic Stroke
academic.summary: Automated polysomnography after ischemic stroke is challenging because of altered sleep-related neural activity and concurrent respiratory disturbances. Existing stroke-specific approaches mainly address sleep-stage classification, leaving joint analysis of sleep architecture and respiratory events underexplored. Moreover, adapting pretrained EEG encoders introduces a representation inconsistency when downstream models are trained on embeddings from previously seen patients but evaluated on unseen individuals. We propose MM-Net, a multimodal multi-task framework that resolves this inconsistency through cross-fitting and ridge-based embedding alignment. Sleep-adapted EEG-EOG representations and engineered neural descriptors are fused with learned cardiorespiratory features through cross-attention and shared temporal modeling for simultaneous sleep staging and respiratory-event detection. On iSLEEPS (99 patients with subacute ischemic stroke), ten-fold patient-independent evaluation achieved 76.3% staging accuracy (Cohen's $κ$ = 0.656) and 0.825 respiratory-event AUC, outperforming the evaluated baselines under matched protocols. The sleep-adapted encoder improved the downstream model when its embeddings were aligned, raising staging accuracy by 1.4 percentage points over the frozen encoder ($p$ = 0.020) versus 0.2 points without alignment. MM-Net also achieved 86.4% staging accuracy on Sleep-EDF, above every single-EEG architecture reimplemented on the same recordings, and 80.3% staging accuracy with 0.889 respiratory AUC on ISRUC-I, exceeding its retrained staging baselines. Without retraining, the iSLEEPS-trained model retained respiratory AUCs of 0.833 on ISRUC-I and 0.841 on UCD. These findings support representation-consistent neural adaptation and joint physiological modeling across stroke, healthy-sleep, and sleep-disorder cohorts.

academic.title: The Metrology Atlas: describing recorded physiological data as a measurement system, with VitalDB as a first application
academic.summary: Every value in a recorded physiological dataset is a pair: a recorded time and a recorded value. Neither is the truth. The time comes from a clock that drifts and is corrected in jumps, and often describes a window that ended earlier. The value was quantised, rounded, sometimes heaped by hand, and measured by an instrument with its own error. We present the Metrology Atlas, a dataset-independent way of describing a recorded dataset as a measurement system, and its first application, to VitalDB, an open dataset of 6,388 surgical patients, as a proof of principle. For every variable, the atlas states what was measured, the measurement model linking it to the recorded pair, and what is known about the true time and true value given a record. Each part of the model carries its evidence: 69 studies, 49 parameters and 54 observations, each marked as measured, derived, estimated or assumed. The atlas maps 11 clocks and 14 devices into one timing network, and closes loops in that network to test its own model. Synchronisation reduces the median timing error between the EEG and ECG from 794 ms to 42 ms, and between ventilator and monitor waveforms from 378 ms to 55 ms. The atlas also documents data-quality issues, several of which correct the dataset's own documentation. It is published as a website and a single machine-readable file, with open-source code and a scheme of time-aware labels. Everything is open under CC BY 4.0 and MIT licences. The engine, schema and timing tools carry over unchanged, and the aim is to describe many other datasets the same way.

academic.title: Interaction-Gated Time-Frequency Learning for Parameter-Efficient PPG-Based Heart Rate Estimation
academic.summary: Photoplethysmography (PPG) enables low-cost and non-invasive heart rate (HR) monitoring but remains sensitive to waveform distortion, physiological variability, and measurement interference. Temporal waveform characteristics and frequency-domain periodicity provide complementary information for HR estimation; however, effectively exploring and integrating these representations within a compact model remains challenging. This paper proposes TF-IG, a parameter-efficient interaction-gated time-frequency learning framework for PPG-based HR estimation. TF-IG employs a dual-branch architecture in which a temporal branch captures pulse morphology via dilated depthwise-separable convolutions, while a frequency branch extracts cardiac periodicity information from bounded log-spectrogram representations. To combine the two domains, we introduce an interaction-gated fusion module that explicitly models feature agreement and discrepancy, while also learning feature-wise weights to balance temporal and spectral information. A parameter-shared regression head further maps the temporal, spectral, and fused representations into the final HR prediction space. Experiments on the benchmark BIDMC PPG and Respiration Dataset using a subject-exclusive training, validation, and test protocol show that TF-IG achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.227 BPM, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 2.060 BPM, a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.9934, and 92.28 percent of estimates within 3 BPM, while remaining parameter-efficient with only 84.6K parameters. Ablation results further demonstrate the complementary contributions of the temporal and frequency branches, interaction-gated fusion, and shared regression head. These results indicate that explicitly modeling cross-domain interactions provides an effective accuracy-complexity trade-off for lightweight PPG-based HR estimation.

academic.title: ECG-SDI: Single-lead Electrocardiogram Enables Continuous Sleep Depth Index Profiling and Scalable Digital Biomarkers for Sleep Health
academic.summary: Conventional sleep staging provides a coarse-grained representation that obscures within-stage depth variation. We developed ECG-SDI, a single-lead electrocardiography (ECG) framework for continuous sleep-depth profiling and digital biomarker extraction. Using 12,392 overnight polysomnographic recordings, we trained and validated a two-stage deep learning model supervised by conventional sleep-stage labels. Correlations with ordered stages excluding rapid eye movement (REM) sleep were 0.828 in the pooled internal test set and 0.848 in the external Cleveland Family Study; corresponding REM classification AUROCs were 0.954 and 0.977. Overnight trajectories captured within-stage variation. Biomarker-based phenotyping identified a disturbed subtype associated with poorer subjective sleep quality and higher all-cause mortality in the Sleep Heart Health Study (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.20; 95% CI, 1.05-1.38). Among 507 participants with paired recordings before and after continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), normalized sleep-depth area increased by 6.1% and shallow-sleep burden below 0.3 decreased by 16.0%. Exploratory analyses linked reductions in approximate entropy and depth variability to reduced oxygen desaturation and increased sleep efficiency, respectively (Spearman rho = 0.24 and 0.12); both associations remained positive after covariate adjustment. Mean ECG-SDI within N2 increased by 0.017 (95% CI, 0.004-0.030). A wearable proof-of-concept illustrated the acquisition-to-report workflow. These findings support ECG-based sleep phenotyping and further evaluation of CPAP response monitoring at home.
